summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically; United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

Same-sex sexual activity is lawful for men and women. Criminalisation ended before 1983, when the age of consent was set at 21 in line with the United Kingdom; the male same-sex age of consent fell to 18 in 2000 and was equalised at 16 by legislation approved in 2011 that took effect on 5 November 2012. Guernsey retains specific male homosexual offences, including a ban on homosexual sexual acts not conducted in private. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can therefore face prosecution for conduct that is lawful in the United Kingdom.

Transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 2007, including obtaining a new birth certificate. The law permits only the issue of a new certificate and does not amend or remove entries from the existing record, so prior gender markers remain visible on the original document. A visitor carrying both records, or documents issued at different times, should expect the earlier marker to remain on file.

The States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage on 10 December 2015 by 37 votes to 7, rejecting a civil-partnership-only scheme and a single secular status called Union Civile as insufficient. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill and commenced in 2018. Guernsey is the only part of the British Isles never to have enacted its own civil partnership legislation; United Kingdom civil partnerships have been recognised for succession purposes since 2 April 2012.

A review of the Adoption Law, recorded at page 1170 of the Billet d'État of 24 June 2015, ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting. The States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised in adoption proceedings, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

Discrimination protections were built in stages. A 2004 law enabled the States to pass Ordinances banning discrimination, and the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005 prohibited discrimination based on gender identity in employment. As of 2020 no equivalent Ordinance had outlawed discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation. Protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity have applied in child welfare proceedings in Guernsey and Alderney since 2008 and in Sark since 2016. In September 2022 the States passed a comprehensive anti-discrimination bill unanimously, 33 votes to 0, explicitly including sexual orientation and rejecting proposed exemptions for businesses of five employees or fewer and for religious affiliations. It took effect on 1 October 2023.

Les Nicolles, Guernsey's only prison, opened in 1989 and holds male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages across 11 wings, with a capacity of 139 and about 99 prisoners in November 2024. No rule on housing prisoners by birth sex versus gender identity, no separate unit for trans prisoners, and no solitary or segregation practice for them is recorded in the available sources, so a trans visitor has no sourced assurance about placement if detained.
tangentialFactors:
Jersey approved the same adoption change two days before Guernsey, on 24 June 2015, extending adoption to same-sex couples with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners.

Guernsey's anti-discrimination settlement rests on local Ordinances rather than the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, and the 2025 single-sex services code issued under that Act has no force in the islands.

The retained offence of homosexual acts not conducted in private has no counterpart in the United Kingdom's modern statute book, so conduct that is lawful at home can remain prosecutable in Guernsey.
localsOnly:
The comprehensive anti-discrimination Act passed in September 2022 by 33 votes to 0 took effect on 1 October 2023. It explicitly covers sexual orientation and rejected amendments exempting businesses of five employees or fewer and organisations with religious affiliations. Gender identity had been protected in employment since the Sex Discrimination (Employment) (Guernsey) Ordinance, 2005.

Same-sex couples may adopt in Guernsey, civil partnerships are recognised in adoption proceedings, and both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

Guernsey adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules on 23 September 2011, making gay and bisexual men eligible after a twelve-month deferral from around 7 November 2011 and ending a local ban dating from the 1980s HIV era. Other donation restrictions were unchanged.

No local civil partnership scheme exists. Residents who want a formalised relationship short of marriage rely on marriage, which commenced in 2018, or on a United Kingdom civil partnership recognised for succession purposes since 2 April 2012.
outOfScopeNotes:
No published rule or policy on how Les Nicolles houses trans prisoners by birth sex or gender identity was identified, and no separate unit or segregation practice is recorded. Placement if a trans visitor is detained is unresolved.

No trans-specific hate-crime statistics, recorded incidents, or enforcement data under the 2023 anti-discrimination Act were identified for Guernsey.

No sourced provision governs access by trans people to bathrooms, changing rooms or other single-sex facilities in Guernsey, and the United Kingdom's 2025 single-sex services code does not extend to the islands.

Whether the 2023 Act's gender-identity coverage extends beyond employment, and any case law or tribunal decisions under it, is not sourced.

No data on trans-specific violence in Guernsey was identified.
